title: Theory of Attachment and Place Attachment

findings.antecedent: Places (where people are born, live, and act)
findings.quote: The theme of this chapter has its general reference frame in that sector of human experience represented by affect – feelings, moods, emotions, etc. – which people experience in various ways, forms, degrees, with varying awareness, with reference to the places in which they are born, live and act.

findings.antecedent: Affective feeling towards places and communities
findings.quote: The feeling we experience towards certain places and to the communities that the places help to define and that are themselves defined by the places... certainly has a strong positive effect in defining our identity...

findings.antecedent: Equal attachment to the same place (by different groups)
findings.quote: These conflicts stem from an equal attachment to the same place, which puts them in competition.
the phenomenon was long considered to be of secondary importance vis-à-vis the primary objective of studying the cognitive and behavioural aspects of such relationships.
Attachment behaviour of the child finds its complement in the mother's protective behaviour.
When the child has a "secure base" to rely on, he is free to move away from it and explore the environment.

The formation of an affective bond seems mainly to be a function of the richness of the social interaction (intensity and quality of the interaction) with the person(s) towards whom the attachment behaviour is directed
It seems even that the stronger and healthier the attachment to the main figure, the more likely there are to be secondary attachments (Bowlby, 1969, p. 308).
The relationship with the attachment figure tends to persist also under unfavourable environmental conditions, such as abuse and ill treatment...

findings.antecedent: Forced transfer from place of residence
findings.consequent: Interruption in sense of continuity, fragmentation of spatial and group identity
findings.quote: the forced transfer from the place of residence represented an interruption in the individuals' sense of continuity, in that it involved the fragmentation of two essential components of identity, namely spatial identity and group identity, which are associated with strong affective elements.

findings.consequent: Feeling of belongingness and sorrow at moving out
findings.quote: length of residence seems to be closely linked both to the feeling of belongingness and to the sorrow at moving out of the community – both of which are also age-linked
It is the emotional significance that geographic spaces are able to take on in human experience that transforms them into “places”.

findings.consequent: Attachment to place (as a fundamental human need)
findings.quote: Attachment to place is considered a fundamental human need (Relph, 1976)

findings.antecedent: Spatial uniformity, increased mobility, and functionalistic relationship with places (in contemporary society)
findings.consequent: Inability to satisfy need for attachment to place
findings.quote: contemporary society is increasingly unable to satisfy [the need for attachment to place] owing to its tendency towards gradual spatial uniformity, increased mobility and hence a purely functionalistic relationship with places.

findings.antecedent: Strong affective ties with place of residence
findings.consequent: Dysfunctional outcomes, precluding adaptation to new opportunities
findings.quote: strong affective ties with the place of residence may to some extent prove dysfunctional, precluding adaptation to new opportunities

the functional value of the attachment bond can be identified as the promotion of residential stability until such time as the latter remains rewarding, while attachment is believed to decline when the place is no longer able to satisfy the inhabitant's needs.

findings.antecedent: Congruity between needs and environmental resources
findings.quote: In positive cases attachment is developed, whereas in the case of incongruity, the individuals will either not form attachments or be repulsed.

findings.consequent: Intensity of attachment to place of residence
findings.quote: a positive correlation between length of residence and the intensity of attachment to the place of residence is a widely reported finding
affective investment... is comparatively unaffected by the length of residence.

findings.consequent: Greater desire for stability in adulthood
findings.quote: a high degree of mobility during childhood is associated with a greater desire for stability in adulthood

findings.antecedent: Environments experienced in childhood or adolescence
findings.quote: Strong positive affective bonds seem to develop towards the environments experienced in childhood or adolescence, and more occasionally towards environments experienced only in adulthood.

findings.consequent: Capacity to form attachments in adulthood
findings.quote: unsatisfactory residential experiences occurring during infancy and adolescence seem to have negative long-term consequences on the capacity to form attachments in adulthood, even towards the more satisfactory environments.

findings.consequent: Stronger feelings of attachment, expression of individual identity
findings.quote: primary territories are better able to express individual identity and are characterised by stronger feelings of attachment
not all forms of attachment – in particular that associated with the expression of identity – demand a long term experience with place
for the vast majority the place of greatest affection is one's birthplace
a high index of mobility is associated with an increased presence of symptoms of malaise, but also that the relationship between mobility and health is not always negative.

findings.antecedent: Less opportunity for choice (obliged to live in unsatisfactory environment)
findings.quote: Persons with less opportunity for choice who are obliged to live in an environment that does not come up to their expectations are more likely to have health problems than those with a high residential mobility.

the feeling of security is perceived as particularly important by the younger children (less than 13 years old) and is not a function of the physical protection offered by the home but of permanence (in Bowlbian terms we could say of accessibility).

findings.consequent: Stronger attachment to home (driven by need for security/protection)
findings.quote: the stronger attachment the elderly display towards the home might thus be seen as the re-emergence of the dominant need for security and protection.
the stronger attachment to the neighbourhood found among the lower classes might be accounted for by the continued activation of stress reducing behaviours connected with poverty of resources
